title: AI Governance, Security and Costs
promise: Know what AI is used in your organization, with what data, how much it costs, and who is accountable for each thing: a usage policy, permissions, spending limits, and a monthly audit that actually happens.
audience: managers, administration, IT or compliance leads at SMEs, schools, associations and institutions where AI already got in without asking permission
plain: This is about putting an adult in the room. In almost every organization AI is already inside: someone summarizes minutes with ChatGPT on their personal account, someone else pasted the customer list into a tool they tried out one weekend, there are three paid subscriptions and nobody knows who uses them, and the day something goes wrong nobody will know what was being used or with what data. This kit doesn't ban or preach: it puts things in order. First an honest inventory of what's really being used (amnesty included, because without amnesty people lie); then a one-page usage policy people can actually follow (what's okay, what isn't, what data never leaves); a permissions matrix that says who can use what with what data; an onboarding circuit so trying a new tool is easy and gets logged; spending limits with a warning before the shock on the invoice; a risk and incident log that turns scares into lessons; and a thirty-minute monthly audit that keeps all of the above alive. The proof it works isn't the paperwork: it's that asking for permission costs less than skipping it, and that leadership can answer in two minutes: "what AI do you use and what does it cost?"
fits: AI is already being used freely across your organization and nobody has the full picture
Someone pasted customer or student data into a free tool and you found out late (or you're afraid you will)
There are several paid AI subscriptions (some duplicated, some abandoned) and no purchasing criteria
Leadership asks "how much do we spend on AI and for what?" and the answer takes a week
A client, a board, or an administration asks in writing how you use AI and what controls you have
You want to allow AI with judgment in a school or an entity that handles sensitive data
An API bill spiked one month and it was discovered when the charge arrived
Every team picked its own tool and there are five different ways of doing the same thing
Someone leaves and nobody knows what accounts, keys and automations they leave behind
You're going to sell AI services and need to be able to show a client how you govern your own
notFor: Drafting formal compliance with the AI Act for high-risk systems (biometrics, personnel selection, credit scoring): that's specialist work; this kit leaves you the inventory and log they'll ask for on day one
Organizations where nobody with authority is going to back the policy: governance with no leadership behind it is just another PDF in a folder
Monitoring employees under the excuse of AI control: this governs tools and data, not people; if the goal is to monitor people, this isn't the kit or the spirit
Banning everything: if the conclusion you're after is "no AI here," you don't need a kit, you need a sentence (and to brace for the shadow use that sentence guarantees)
Replacing legal advice on data protection: the kit organizes and documents; sensitive processing gets reviewed by someone with a signature

scopes.label: Minimum
scopes.what: The usage inventory built with amnesty, the one-page policy approved and communicated, the list of data that never leaves, and accounts and keys put in order (personal accounts out for work use). All in one sheet and one document.
scopes.time: A week in spare moments, 8-10 hours
scopes.cost: €0 in tools: this is people's work
scopes.skip: Skip the onboarding circuit and the formal audit: with the inventory, policy and organized keys you've already removed the three big risks.

scopes.label: Standard
scopes.what: Everything in Minimum plus the permissions matrix by role and data type, the onboarding circuit with logged evaluation and approval (this kit's workflow), spending limits with alerts at every provider, the risk and incident log, and the thirty-minute monthly audit with its minutes.
scopes.time: Three weeks in spare moments, about 20-25 hours
scopes.cost: €0-20/month: n8n if you don't already have it, and cents of API cost for the circuit
scopes.skip: Skip the consolidated spend dashboard: with per-provider limits and alerts plus the monthly review you go plenty far at the start.

scopes.label: Advanced
scopes.what: Everything above plus a consolidated spend dashboard by system and team, quarterly policy review with the quarter's incidents, documented vendor evaluations (where they process, what they sign), annual training for the team, and the governance report ready to show clients or auditors.
scopes.skip: Don't start here: governance earns its authority by solving the basics well. A beautiful dashboard on top of a dishonest inventory is theater.

brief.name: Define governance before writing a single rule
brief.when: First thing. Before drafting the policy, before banning anything, before buying any control tool.
brief.prompt:
Act as a pragmatic technology governance consultant for small organizations, allergic to decorative bureaucracy. We're going to set up my organization's AI governance (policy, permissions, spending, risks, audit) and I want you to force me to design it to fit us, not to copy a multinational's.

My context:
- Organization, size and what it does: [ORGANIZATION]
- What AI I know (or suspect) is used today, officially and off the books: [CURRENT USE]
- What data the organization handles and which is sensitive: [DATA]
- What keeps me up at night: the incident I fear most, or the one that already happened: [FEARS]
- Who would be in charge of this: who can approve a policy and enforce it: [AUTHORITY]
- What we spend on AI today, even roughly (subscriptions + API): [SPEND]
- House culture: do people ask permission or ask forgiveness?: [CULTURE]
- External obligations: clients, administration or sector requirements: [EXTERNAL]

Do this, in this order:

1. Give me my situation back as a three-column map: what's already fine (even if informal), the holes that could hurt (data, spend, accounts), and what's noise (things that look urgent and aren't). Flag with WARNING anything you're assuming.
2. Ask me only the three questions that would most change the design. Stop dead and wait for my answer.
3. Once I answer, give me the order of attack: which piece of governance to build first based on MY holes, not a manual's table of contents. If my biggest hole is personal accounts with customer data, the policy can wait a week; that can't.
4. Tell me what NOT to regulate: which uses are so harmless that putting them through the circuit only creates paperwork and disobedience. Governance that regulates everything governs nothing.
5. Propose the right size for each piece for my organization: how many pages of policy, how many permission levels, how often the audit. Justify it with my size and my culture.
6. Write the three-month success criteria with observable numbers: percentage of real usage that's in the inventory, days it takes to decide an onboarding request, billing shocks (should be zero), and the litmus test: does asking permission cost less than skipping it?

Don't give me the policy yet. Don't give me templates yet. If you think my organization doesn't need this (we're three people and we talk to each other), tell me and give me the one-afternoon version.

fill.what: Who you are and how many people
fill.example: State-subsidized training center, 40 employees between teaching staff and administration

fill.what: The official and the suspected, without polishing it
fill.example: Official: two Copilot licenses. Off the books: personal ChatGPT in the front office and several teachers, and someone set up an n8n

fill.what: What data exists and which of it burns
fill.example: Minor students' data, academic records, payroll; the sensitive part: minors and health (accommodations)
A teacher pasting a list of students with diagnoses into a free tool
The director, with the leadership team behind her
About €60/month in known subscriptions; no idea if there are loose APIs
Asks forgiveness: people solve things on their own and mention it afterward, if they mention it
Educational inspection, families, and the regional authority if there's an incident with minors' data

brief.expect: The three-column map with warnings, three questions, the order of attack based on your holes, the list of what not to regulate, the right-sized pieces, and the success criteria with the litmus test.
brief.stuck: If it hands back a corporate governance plan with committees and acronyms, stop it: "we are [n] people; give me the version that fits our week." And if your culture asks forgiveness, take that seriously in the design: the onboarding circuit has to be faster than the shortcut, or nobody will use it.

architecture.what: The real picture: what AI tools and automations are used, by whom, for what, with what data and with what account.
architecture.nocode: A sheet with one row per system or use, gathered through interviews and declared amnesty.
architecture.code: The same table, cross-checked against card charges and domain sign-ups to catch what the interviews miss.
architecture.why: You can't govern what you can't see. And without explicit amnesty ("whatever comes up now has no consequences") the inventory comes out false, because people hide what they're afraid will be taken away.

architecture.what: The page that says what's allowed, what's forbidden, and what data never leaves, in plain human language.
architecture.nocode: A one-page document (two at most) approved by leadership and explained in a short session.
architecture.code: The same document, versioned, with a change log.
architecture.why: A twenty-page policy nobody reads, and a one-page one gets followed. The heart of it is the list of data that never leaves: it's what people remember at the moment of pasting.

architecture.what: Who can use what, with what type of data, and who approves exceptions: the policy turned into a table.
architecture.nocode: A two-way table: roles as rows, usage levels as columns (general use with no data, internal data, personal data, sensitive data).
architecture.code: The same matrix applied to groups and permissions in the tools where possible.
architecture.why: "It depends on who and what data" is the right answer to almost everything, and the matrix turns it into something checkable in ten seconds instead of a call to the boss.

architecture.what: How you request a new tool or a new use: a short request, evaluation against the policy, a logged decision.
architecture.nocode: This kit's workflow: form, AI evaluation against your policy, human approval, and entry into the inventory.
architecture.code: The same circuit on the ticketing system if one already exists.
architecture.why: The circuit is what keeps the inventory alive without a police force: if asking is easy and fast (days, not weeks, for an answer), people ask; if it's an ordeal, the shadow use comes back.

architecture.what: Every professional use on an organizational account, keys in the password manager, and the two-person rule for critical access.
architecture.nocode: Migration from personal to corporate accounts, a team password manager, and a list of who has what.
architecture.code: API keys per system (not one for everything), named to show what they belong to, with rotation noted.
architecture.why: The personal account is risk number one: the person leaves and the access, history, and sometimes the data leave with them. And a single shared API key for everything makes it impossible to know which system spent what.

architecture.what: A budget per system, hard limits or alerts configured at each provider, and actual spend noted each month.
architecture.nocode: Each provider's dashboard limits and alerts, plus a spend tab in the inventory sheet.
architecture.code: The same plus reading consumption via API wherever the provider offers it.
architecture.why: The billing shock always has the same anatomy: a loop, a forgotten test, or an expensive model where a cheap one was needed, discovered when the charge lands. The limit set up on day one of onboarding costs two minutes and kills the whole genre.

architecture.what: The living list of what can go wrong (with an owner and mitigation) and the notebook of what actually went wrong (no blame, with lessons).
architecture.nocode: Two more tabs in the sheet: risks with owner and status, and incidents with what happened, what was done, and what changed.
architecture.code: The same; the value is in the habit, not the tool.
architecture.why: An incident log with no witch hunt is what makes people report scares on time. An incident reported on day one is a lesson; hidden for three months, it's a file.

architecture.what: The thirty minutes a month that keep everything above alive: inventory against reality, spend against budget, risks and pending requests.
architecture.nocode: A monthly appointment with this kit's checklist and a ten-line record.
architecture.code: The workflow that gathers the data and drafts the minutes before the meeting.
architecture.why: All governance decays without rhythm: the inventory goes stale, the limits get outdated, the risks get forgotten. The short monthly audit isn't a control: it's the maintenance that avoids rebuilding everything every year.

stack.need: The inventory, the matrix and the logs
stack.nocode: A single Google Sheet with tabs: systems, requests, spend, risks, incidents, audits.
stack.code: The same tables in the house database if one already exists.
stack.pick: A sheet, no doubt about it: leadership has to be able to read the governance without asking for help. A sophisticated GRC tool is for a different scale.

stack.need: The policy and the meeting minutes
stack.nocode: Google Docs or Notion: the versioned policy, one record per audit.
stack.code: Markdown in a repository if the house already lives in Git.
stack.pick: Wherever the team already reads. A policy linked from where people work (the intranet, the pinned general channel) is worth double a correct policy sitting dead in a folder.

stack.nocode: This kit's workflow in n8n: form, evaluation, approval, inventory.
stack.code: The same circuit in the ticketing system if one already has forms.
stack.pick: n8n if there's nothing yet: it's set up in an afternoon and leaves the trail in the same inventory sheet. What matters is the response deadline, not the tool.

stack.nocode: HTTP calls to the Anthropic API from n8n, with the policy inside the prompt.
stack.pick: A mid-size model: evaluating a request against a one-page policy is fine-grained but short work. The decision is always human: the AI prepares the file.

stack.nocode: A team password manager (free and cheap ones exist) with folders per system.
stack.code: The same plus environment variables and CI secrets for the technical side.
stack.pick: Any decent shared manager beats the best individual system. The two-person rule for critical access isn't negotiable: it's what prevents accidental hostage-taking by vacation or leave.

stack.nocode: Slack for onboarding approval and spend alerts; email if leadership doesn't use Slack.
stack.pick: Wherever the approver answers within hours. The onboarding circuit lives or dies by its response time: pick the channel by real speed, not elegance.

fields: What it is: the tool or automation, with a recognizable name
The specific use, in one sentence
Who uses it: people or team
Who's accountable for it: a person, not a department
Level of data it touches: none, internal, personal, sensitive
What account it's used with (always corporate; if it says personal, that's a finding)
What it costs per month: subscription or API budget
The configured spend limit or alert, and where
When it's due for review (renewal, vendor evaluation)
data.note: The data column is the one that matters: it's the one that crosses with the permissions matrix and decides how much attention each row deserves. An image generator with no data and a workflow that reads students' email don't play in the same league.

fields: The intended use, in their own words
What data it would touch: none, internal, personal, sensitive
What the evaluation ruled: fits, fits with conditions, doesn't fit
The conditions of use if any (no personal data, corporate account, spending limit X)
data.note: The lag between date and decision is the circuit's vital sign: if it runs past a few days, people will go back to the shortcut. Measure it at every monthly audit.

fields: What can go wrong, in one concrete sentence ("student data pasted into an unauthorized tool")
Which system or use it affects, or 'general'
high, medium, low: how much it would hurt if it happens
high, medium, low: how much you'd bet this happens this year
What's been done or decided so it doesn't happen (or hurts less)
data.note: The accepted status is legitimate and valuable: "we know, it's not worth mitigating, we sign off" is an adult decision. What's not legitimate is a risk with no owner: that's the one that materializes some August.

phases.title: Inventory with amnesty and one-page policy
phases.goal: See everything that's really being used and publish a policy people can follow, with leadership behind it.
phases.deliverable: The complete system inventory and the usage policy, approved, communicated and linked where the team works.
done: The inventory has one row per real use, including those that surfaced through amnesty
Each row has a named owner and an assigned data level
The policy fits on one page, leadership has signed it, and the team has heard it explained
The list of data that never leaves is in the policy and on a separate, visible poster

steps.title: Run the kickoff brief with the truth
steps.action: Fill in the kickoff prompt without dressing up the shadow use or the house culture. Answer the three questions and keep the order of attack.
steps.expect: The map of your situation, the order of attack based on your holes, and the right size for each piece.
steps.stuck: If you catch yourself describing the organization as it should be instead of as it is, start with the fear: the incident you dread tells more truth about your house than the org chart.

steps.title: Build the inventory with declared amnesty
steps.where: With people, not a cold form
steps.action: Announce the amnesty ("we want to put this in order, nobody loses anything by reporting what they use") and use the inventory prompt to prep short per-team interviews. Fill in the systems tab with each use that surfaces.
steps.expect: More rows than you expected, including two or three that surprise you. That's the sign the amnesty worked.
steps.stuck: If little surfaces, people haven't believed the amnesty: have leadership announce it in person, and start by admitting what you personally use, warts and all. Honesty flows downhill.

steps.title: Write the one-page policy
steps.action: Use the policy prompt with your inventory and your real sensitive data. Trim until it fits one page. Bring it to leadership to fight over and sign.
steps.expect: One page with: what's okay, what isn't, the list of data that never leaves, the accounts rule, and how to request something new. Signed.
steps.stuck: If leadership wants to add legal-umbrella paragraphs, defend the page: every paragraph added costs readers. The umbrella goes in an appendix lawyers will read; the page is for people.

steps.title: Communicate it like something important
steps.where: A short session with the team, not an email
steps.action: Fifteen minutes live: why it exists, the three rules that matter, the list of data that never leaves, and the key message: asking is easy and the past isn't punished. Leave the policy linked where the team works.
steps.expect: Uncomfortable questions live (a good sign) and the policy a click away for everyone.
steps.stuck: The question that will come up: "so can I keep using X?" Have the answer ready with phase 2's matrix in hand, or an honest "that's exactly what we're solving this week."

phases.title: Permissions matrix and onboarding circuit
phases.goal: Make "can I use this?" answerable in ten seconds with the matrix, and requesting something new cost two minutes and get decided in days.
phases.deliverable: The published permissions matrix and the onboarding circuit working, with evaluation, logged approval, and an inventory that feeds itself.
done: The matrix crosses roles with data levels and fits on half a page
The request form exists and the team knows where it is
A test request has gone through the whole circuit: evaluation, decision, entry in the inventory
The agreed decision deadline is written down and the approver knows it

steps.title: Build the permissions matrix
steps.where: A sheet, with the policy in front of you
steps.action: Rows: your house's real roles (not theoretical titles). Columns: usage levels (no data, internal data, personal data, sensitive data). In each cell: allowed, allowed with conditions (which), or requires approval (from whom).
steps.expect: Half a page that answers 90% of the doubts without asking anyone. Almost all the sensitive-data cells in "requires approval": correct.
steps.stuck: If you end up with eight roles and six levels, you're photographing the org chart, not the usage: group by how people actually work. Three or four roles are enough in almost any SME.

steps.title: Import the onboarding circuit
steps.action: Import this kit's workflow, connect credentials (Sheets, Slack and the model), and paste your policy and matrix into the evaluation node's prompt. Create the request form pointing at the webhook.
steps.expect: The workflow active and the form working: request → evaluation against YOUR policy → approval on Slack → inventory.
steps.stuck: The typical mistake: leaving a generic policy in the prompt. The evaluation is only as good as the policy pasted inside it; if it evaluates against generalities, it will rule on generalities.

steps.title: Calibrate the evaluation with real cases
steps.action: Run five test requests: a clear fit, one that fits with conditions, one that doesn't fit (sensitive data to a free tool), a vague one, and a trick one (asks to skip the policy). Tune the node's prompt until all five are ruled correctly.
steps.expect: Five correct rulings with concrete conditions. The vague one comes back asking for information, not guessing.
steps.stuck: If the evaluation is too soft (everything fits), add your two or three literal red lines with examples to the prompt. If it's too harsh (everything needs approval), remind it of the principle: the circuit exists to enable, not to block.

steps.title: Agree and publish the decision deadline
steps.action: Agree on the maximum response time to a request (two or three business days is reasonable) and a backup if the approver is out. Write it into the policy and into the form's confirmation message.
steps.expect: A public deadline commitment. It's the clause that makes the whole circuit believable.
steps.stuck: If the approver can't commit to days, it's a design problem: lower the bar on what needs their approval (more matrix cells at "allowed with conditions") and reserve them for sensitive data only.

steps.title: Migrate accounts and organize keys
steps.where: Every tool in the inventory, one by one
steps.action: Go through the inventory: every professional use moves to a corporate account, keys go into the manager with a clear name, every critical access has two people, and orphaned subscriptions (nobody uses them) get cancelled today.
steps.expect: Zero personal accounts in the account column, the manager populated, and probably €10-30/month of dead subscriptions recovered: the kit starts paying for itself.
steps.stuck: There will be resistance about personal accounts ("I lose my history"). Offer the migration with help and no rush, but with a date. A personal account with organizational data isn't a preference: it's the inventory's risk number one.

phases.title: Spending limits and measurement
phases.goal: Make sure no AI charge is a surprise: budget per system, limits or alerts at every provider, and actual spend noted each month.
phases.deliverable: Every system with a limit or alert configured, the spend tab up to date, and an annual AI budget presentable to leadership.
done: Every paid system in the inventory has its limit or alert configured, noted where
The spend tab has last month's actuals, system by system
An annual budget exists, with a growth scenario
A spend alert has been simulated and reached the right person

steps.title: Set budget and limit for each system
steps.where: Each provider's dashboard and the sheet
steps.action: With the spending-limits prompt, decide the monthly budget for each system in the inventory and configure a hard limit or an 80% alert at each provider. Note in the row where each is configured.
steps.expect: No paid row without a limit or alert. Where a provider offers neither, note it as a risk: it's a data point for choosing a provider next time.
steps.stuck: For APIs, the doubt is how much to set: look at the last few months' spend and set double as the alert and quadruple as the hard limit. You'll adjust with data; what matters is that it exists.

steps.title: Set up monthly spend logging
steps.action: One row per system and month: budgeted, actual, deviation. The actual comes from invoices and dashboards; fifteen minutes a month. It's part of the monthly audit.
steps.expect: The first month logged. By three months you have a trend; by six, the ability to forecast.
steps.stuck: If gathering the invoices takes more than fifteen minutes, the problem is scattered accounts: centralize AI payments on one card or account and the invoices land in one place by themselves.

steps.title: Simulate the shock to test the alerts
steps.action: Temporarily lower an alert below current spend and check the warning reaches the right person (not an inbox nobody watches). Restore the value and note the result.
steps.expect: The alert received by someone who can act. A limit that warns an orphaned inbox is a decorative limit.
steps.stuck: If the provider only alerts the account holder and the holder isn't the one watching, redirect: an email rule forwarding billing alerts to the alerts channel. Inelegant, works.

steps.title: Prepare a defensible annual budget
steps.where: Claude, with the spend tab in front of you
steps.action: With the second part of the limits prompt: the annual budget per system, the scenario if usage grows, and the three possible savings decisions (consolidate duplicate subscriptions, downgrade the model where it isn't noticed, turn off what isn't used).
steps.expect: One page of budget leadership understands: what exists, what it will cost, where it can be trimmed without losing anything.
steps.stuck: If there's no history to budget from, say so in the document: "starting budget, reviewed with real data this quarter." An honest budget with an announced review beats a precise, invented one.

phases.title: Risks, monthly audit and handoff
phases.goal: Turn scares into a log, oversight into a thirty-minute ritual, and governance into something that doesn't depend on you.
phases.deliverable: The risk log with owners, two monthly audits done with their minutes, and a governance folder that can be shown to a third party.
done: The risk log has the first ten with impact, probability, mitigation and owner
The incident log exists and the team knows reporting a scare costs nothing
Two monthly audits done, with ten-line minutes and at least one action each
Someone else has run the second audit with the checklist, without you

steps.title: Build the risk log
steps.where: Claude, and half an hour with leadership
steps.action: With the risk-log prompt and your inventory in front of you, pull out the concrete risks in YOUR house, score them, and assign owners. Bring it to leadership to accept or ask to mitigate.
steps.expect: Ten concrete (not generic) risks with an owner and a decision: mitigate, accept, or watch. Signed off.
steps.stuck: If the risks come out textbook ("AI can hallucinate"), go back to the inventory: every good risk comes from a specific row ("workflow X reads inbox Y that contains Z"). The generic can't be mitigated.

steps.title: Kick off the incident log with a real one
steps.action: Note the last scare that happened (there's always one): what happened, what was done, what changes so it doesn't repeat. No names in the cause column: causes, not culprits. Show it as an example of the tone.
steps.expect: A first logged incident that demonstrates the spirit: telling is free, hiding is expensive.
steps.stuck: If nobody remembers any scare, ask the reverse: "what almost happened?" Near-misses are the best material and the cheapest: all the lesson, none of the damage.

steps.title: Run the first monthly audit
steps.where: A thirty-minute appointment, with the checklist
steps.action: With the monthly-audit prompt, generate your checklist and run through it: inventory against reality, spend against budget, requests and their turnaround, risks moving, incidents from the month. Ten-line minutes with the actions.
steps.expect: Thirty minutes, short minutes, and one or two concrete actions with an owner. If it takes two hours, the list is too ambitious: trim it.
steps.stuck: The first audit always finds the inventory already outdated (someone started using something). It's not a failure: it's exactly the mechanism working. Add it to the inventory, and if it didn't go through the circuit, a friendly chat about the form.

steps.title: Prepare the showable governance folder
steps.action: Gather what a client, an auditor or a board would ask for: the signed policy, the matrix, the inventory (a version without sensitive internal data), the risk log, the audit minutes, and the onboarding procedure. An index page up front.
steps.expect: The two-minute answer to "how do you govern your AI?": open the folder and show it. For anyone selling services, this is sales material.
steps.stuck: Don't manufacture documents for the folder you don't actually use: an experienced auditor spots live paper versus prop paper in two questions. The folder is the real governance, organized.

steps.title: Hand off the ritual and let go
steps.where: With whoever will carry on the governance, and the handoff prompt
steps.action: Write the governance handoff sheet with the delivery prompt: what's maintained, at what rhythm, where each piece lives, what to do with a request, a spend scare, or an incident. Have someone else run the second audit with the sheet and the checklist, with you as an observer.
steps.expect: An audit run by someone else with no help from you. Governance that depends on one person is that person's hobby.
steps.stuck: If there's no candidate to inherit the ritual, that's the number-one risk in the log itself: write it there, with leadership as the owner. Governance with no succession plan is the first thing the audit should flag.

prompts.name: Build the usage inventory with amnesty
prompts.when: In phase 1, to prep the interviews and organize what surfaces.
prompts.prompt:
Act as a consultant helping a small organization discover what AI is really being used inside, including what nobody has reported. The goal isn't to catch anyone: it's an honest picture, and amnesty has been declared. Help me prep the fieldwork and organize what comes out of it.

My context:
- Organization and teams: [ORGANIZATION]
- What I already know is used (official): [OFFICIAL]
- What I suspect is used off the books: [SUSPECTED]
- Sensitive data in the house: [DATA]

Give me, in this order:

1. The fifteen-minute interview script per team: the six questions that surface real usage without putting anyone on the defensive. Include the indirect ones that work ("what boring task have you managed to shed this year?", "what tool would you recommend to a new coworker?") and the direct data question ("what's the most sensitive thing that's gone through there?") phrased so it can be answered honestly.
2. The three exact phrases to announce amnesty credibly, and the mistake that kills it (announcing it and then demanding explanations for what surfaces).
3. Where to look for usage the interviews won't reveal: card charges with tool names, email sign-ups with AI-provider domains, installed browser extensions, automations someone built and then left.
4. The structure to organize what comes out: review my columns (name, for_what, who, owner, data, account, cost_month, status) and tell me if MY case is missing one or has an extra, with the reason.
5. Triage criteria for the first pass: which inventory rows demand action this week (hint: sensitive data + free tool + personal account is the fire triplet), which can wait for the normal circuit, and which are harmless and just get noted.
6. How to close each interview leaving the door open: the phrase that gets people to come back and tell you about the use they remembered two days later.

Don't give me a lecture on the risks of shadow AI: I know them, that's why we're doing this. Give me field tools.

fill.what: Who you are and what teams exist
fill.example: Training center, 40 people: teachers, front office, administration and leadership
Two Copilot licenses and a leadership ChatGPT subscription
The front office uses free ChatGPT for letters; some teachers generate exercises; there was an n8n someone left running when they left
Minor students' data, accommodations (health), payroll

prompts.expect: The interview script with the indirect questions, the amnesty phrases, the tracing sites, the validated structure, and the triage with the fire triplet.
prompts.stuck: If the inventory looks thin after the interviews, cross-check with the traces from point 3: the gap between what was reported and what was traced tells you how much trust is still to be earned. Don't turn it into a hunt: turn it into a second round of amnesty.

prompts.name: Write the one-page usage policy
prompts.when: In phase 1, once the inventory is built. Reviewed every quarter with the incidents in front of you.
prompts.prompt:
Act as an internal-policy writer who hates policies nobody reads. We're going to write my organization's AI usage policy: ONE page, human language, followable starting tomorrow. It's not a legal document: it's the house rule, and the legal appendix comes later.

My context:
- Organization: [ORGANIZATION]
- The real usage inventory (summary): [INVENTORY]
- Data that must never leave the house: [FORBIDDEN DATA]
- Tools approved today and with what account: [APPROVED]
- Culture: what rule would actually be followed vs ignored in this house: [CULTURE]
- Who signs the policy: [SIGNATURE]

Write the policy with these exact sections and this spirit:

1. What we use AI for here (three lines): positive and concrete, with two real examples from my inventory. A policy that starts by prohibiting loses the reader on line one.
2. The three golden rules, highlighted: (a) red-list data NEVER gets pasted into any AI tool, with the red list naming my concrete data, not abstract categories; (b) work is done with an organizational account, never personal; (c) whatever AI produces is reviewed by a person before it goes out or is acted on.
3. What you can use without asking permission: the approved tools with their level (refer to the matrix if it exists). Make clear this is most cases: the policy enables more than it restricts.
4. How to request something new: where the form is, how long we take to answer (the agreed, written deadline), and the promise that asking is never penalized.
5. If something goes wrong: report it the same day to [whom], with no fear; we look for causes, not culprits. Two lines, human tone.
6. Validity: who maintains it, when it's reviewed (quarterly), and where the good version lives.

Style rules: informal, short sentences, zero jargon ("AI tool," not "generative AI system"). No "shall be undertaken." prompts.prompt:
Act as a pragmatic risk analyst for small organizations, allergic to generic risk logs written once and never looked at again. We're going to build MY organization's AI risk log, from my real inventory, with owners and decisions.

My data:
- The inventory of systems and uses, with their data level: [INVENTORY]
- The house's sensitive data: [DATA]
- Scares or near-misses we've already had: [SCARES]
- People who could be risk owners: [PEOPLE]
- External obligations (clients, administration, sector): [EXTERNAL]

Do this:

1. Go through my inventory row by row and pull out CONCRETE risks: not "data leak" but "the front-office workflow reads the inbox that receives student accommodations and sends them to a third-party API." Each risk must name the system, the data, and the path of harm. From my past scares, pull out the risk they reveal (a scare is a risk that gave a demo).
2. Add the cross-cutting risks my inventory suggests even if no single row screams them: the person who leaves with everything in their head, the personal account still not migrated, the provider that changes terms, dependence on a single tool for something critical, generated content that goes out unreviewed.
3. Score each one: impact (high/medium/low, based on MY data and MY external exposure) and probability (high/medium/low, based on how my house works). Justify every high score in one sentence.
4. For those in the ugly quadrant (high impact and medium-or-high probability): the cheapest mitigation that drops the quadrant, with its cost in hours or euros. For the rest: mitigate, accept, or watch, with your recommendation and the why in one line.
5. Propose an owner for each risk from my list of people, on the criterion that the owner is whoever would see the signal first, not the highest-ranking boss.
6. Give me the three early-warning signals the monthly audit should watch: the cheap indicators that a risk is heating up.

Fifteen risks max: a fifty-risk log is a log nobody reads. If my inventory gives more, keep the fifteen that matter most and list the rest in one line as "passive watch."

prompts.name: The thirty-minute monthly audit

prompts.prompt:
Act as a pragmatic internal auditor. Design and help me run my organization's monthly AI governance audit: thirty minutes, a fixed checklist, ten-line minutes. The goal isn't finding culprits: it's making sure governance doesn't rot in silence.

This month's data:
- The system inventory (paste the rows or the summary): [INVENTORY]
- This month's requests with their decision dates: [REQUESTS]
- This month's spend against budget, system by system: [SPEND]
- Incidents or scares logged (or the absence of them): [INCIDENTS]
- The risk log, current state: [RISKS]
- What changed in the house this month (people joining or leaving, new projects): [CHANGES]

Run the audit in this order and give me back the result of each point:

1. Inventory against reality: given the month's changes, which inventory rows smell outdated? What likely new use is NOT registered? Give me the two or three concrete questions I should ask this week to check.
2. Onboarding circuit: what was the average decision time this month? If it exceeds the agreed deadline, where did it get stuck? A slow circuit is the prelude to shadow use: treat it as urgent.
3. Spend: the deviations against budget, with your read on each one (healthy growth, new pricing, or a shock forming?). Any paid system with no apparent use? To the cancellation list.
4. Risks: any early-warning signal lit up? Any risk this month's changes moves up or down a quadrant? Are the owners still the right people?
5. Incidents: if any, were they logged with cause and change, no blame? If the month says "zero incidents," uncomfortable question: zero scares or zero trust to report them? Propose how to tell the difference.
6. Accounts and keys: did anyone join or leave the organization this month? Have their access grants and revocations been done?

Close with the ten-line minutes: date, attendees, findings in one line each, and a MAXIMUM of THREE actions with owner and date. More than three actions a month is a recipe for doing zero. If the month is clean, the minutes say so in three lines and move on: the short, honest audit is the one that survives.

prompts.stuck: If the audit gets skipped two months in a row, don't reinforce it: shrink it. Fifteen minutes and four points that actually happen beat thirty-six that don't. And always hold it the same day with the same people: rituals survive by rhythm, not by importance.

prompts.prompt:
Write the operations sheet for a small organization's AI governance, for the person who will maintain it without having built it. Two pages max. It must let them keep the rhythm (requests, spend, incidents, monthly audit) without calling whoever designed it.

Governance system data:
- The pieces and where each lives: [PIECES]
- The onboarding circuit: form, evaluation, who approves, deadline: [ONBOARDING]
- The policy: where it is, who changes it, when it's reviewed: [POLICY]
- Spend: configured limits, monthly logging, budget: [SPEND]
- The risk and incident logs: where and with what tone: [LOGS]
- The monthly audit: day, checklist, minutes: [AUDIT]
- The governance system's own access and keys: [ACCESS]

The sheet has these sections and no more:

1. What this is in five lines: the pieces and why each exists, with the phrase that sums up the spirit ("asking permission must cost less than skipping it").
2. A typical month: what happens on its own, what you do weekly (clear requests within the deadline), and audit day with its checklist. With minutes per task.
3. Clearing a request, step by step: where it arrives, what the evaluation already prepared, what criterion you decide by (the matrix), how you log the decision, and how you communicate the conditions to the requester.
4. The three delicate moments and their script: (a) a spend alert arrives: what to check and when to cut it off; (b) someone reports an incident: how to receive it (thanks, causes, no blame) and what to note; (c) you discover an unregistered use: the friendly conversation that brings it into the inventory without burning the amnesty.
5. The five most likely problems, in a table: signal ("requests are taking a week," "the inventory hasn't been touched in two months," "nobody reports scares"), what it means, and what to do.
6. What NEVER to do: approve a red-list request out of tiredness, use the incident log to point fingers, skip an audit "because there's nothing this month," and change the policy without the signature of whoever signs it.
7. The quarterly review: policy against the quarter's incidents, matrix against reality, and what to bring to leadership.
8. Access: what this person needs to operate and where everything is.

Informal tone, short sentences, every instruction actionable. Tone matters double here: whoever inherits this also inherits the team's trust, and the sheet must convey that governance is a service, not customs control.

costs.free: €0 in tools: sheets and documents you already have.
costs.paid: Nothing, unless you want a paid team password manager (a few euros per user). CHECK THE OFFICIAL WEBSITE.
costs.note: It's the cheapest kit in the catalog in tools and the most expensive in one thing: sticking to the monthly ritual. Budget for the consistency.

costs.free: Self-hosted n8n, €0. Each evaluation is a few thousand tokens: cents per request.
costs.paid: n8n cloud priced by executions if there's no server. CHECK THE OFFICIAL WEBSITE.
costs.note: At ten requests a month, the AI cost of governance is negligible. Its value isn't in what it costs: it's in the response time it achieves.

costs.free: The first cleanup of orphaned and duplicate subscriptions usually recovers €10-50/month: the kit pays for itself in the first month in many houses.
costs.paid: Not applicable: this row is income.
costs.note: Note it in the first audit's minutes: it's the argument that buys leadership's support for everything else.

costs.free: Never zero: the build (about 20-25 hours) and the routine (2-4 hours/month between requests and audit).
costs.paid: Multiply by the hourly cost of whoever runs it. This is the kit's real cost.
costs.note: Compare it to the price of a single data incident or a single billing shock and the math does itself. But do the math: it's your budget argument.

costs.free: There's no free version worth having.
costs.paid: A legal review of the policy and sensitive processing: a few hours of a professional, a few hundred euros well spent.
costs.note: The kit leaves the homework done (inventory, log, policy): a professional review on top of that is cheap. On top of chaos, it's very expensive.

legal: This kit's inventory is the antechamber of the GDPR's records of processing activities: every row with personal data should have its counterpart there, with legal basis, purpose and retention. If it doesn't exist, this inventory is the best starting point for building it.

Every AI provider that touches personal data is a data processor: you need their data processing agreement (serious providers include it in their terms) and to know where they process. Note it in the system's row with the date you checked.

Transfers outside the EU: if the provider processes in the US, rely on the current adequacy framework or standard contractual clauses, and record what you're relying on. It's one line in the system's row; writing it costs a minute, answering for it without it costs weeks.

The free and paid versions of the same provider usually have different terms about how they use your data (including whether they train on it). The policy saying "with a corporate account" isn't red tape: it's usually the difference in terms.

The EU AI Act classifies uses by risk: most of what this kit governs is limited or minimal risk, but if the inventory turns up anything touching personnel selection, evaluation of people, biometrics, or access to essential services, flag it and get specific advice: that plays in a different league.

Duty of information and transparency: if AI participates in communications or decisions affecting people (responses to families, assessments), people should know it and a person must review it. Rule three of the policy ("a person reviews it before it goes out") is also your legal anchor.

Minors' data and special categories: if they're in your house (schools, social organizations, health), the red list isn't a recommendation from this kit, it's your minimization obligation in action. And any incident touching them may be notifiable to the data protection authority within 72 hours: have that written into the incident procedure.

The incident log is a well-wielded double-edged sword: diligently documenting incidents and what changed is exactly what a supervisor wants to see. Hide it or not have it, and the same incident looks far worse.

Ownership and continuity: accounts, keys and subscriptions in the organization's name, with two people per access. It's a business-continuity clause and a compliance clause at once: data in a former employee's personal account is a problem in both categories.

This is practical guidance, not legal advice. The policy, sensitive processing, and any incident involving personal data: get a professional review with a signature. This kit leaves the ground cleared and the bill short.

risks.risk: Governance turns into customs control and the shadow returns
risks.sign: Requests take weeks; people stop asking; the inventory stops growing but real usage keeps growing
risks.fix: The agreed deadline, measured at every audit, plus more matrix cells at "allowed with conditions" and fewer at "requires approval." The circuit competes against the shortcut: it has to win on speed.

risks.risk: Red-list data in a tool with no guarantees
risks.sign: A surfaced use (or an incident) where sensitive data traveled to a free or personal account
risks.fix: Attack the triage's fire triplet (sensitive + free + personal) in the first week; the red list with concrete data in the policy and on a poster; and the incident, if one arrives, into the log and evaluated for whether it needs reporting.

risks.risk: The policy exists and nobody remembers it
risks.sign: Ask three people the three golden rules and you get one and a half back
risks.fix: One page, three rules, explained in person and linked where work happens. And a real memory test every quarter, with a symbolic prize if needed: the policy is what gets remembered.

risks.sign: A charge that multiplies a system's budget
risks.fix: A hard limit in addition to the alert wherever the provider allows it, phase 3's alert drill (did it reach whoever can act?), and the anatomy in the incident log so the same loop doesn't repeat.

risks.risk: The inventory goes stale in silence
risks.sign: Three months with no new rows or changes, in a house where clearly everything gets tried
risks.fix: The monthly audit asks about the month's changes (new people, new projects) and an easy onboarding circuit. A live inventory isn't achieved by watching: it's achieved by making it easy to register.

risks.sign: Zero incidents logged for months, in an organization that uses AI daily
risks.fix: The tone (causes, not culprits) demonstrated with actions the first time someone reports something, and the audit question: zero scares or zero trust? Near-misses are the friendly way in.

risks.sign: Requests pile up and the audit gets skipped two months in a row once the person who built it changes priorities
risks.fix: The handoff sheet, the audit run by someone else as proof, and leadership as owner of the succession risk in the log itself. A thirty-minute ritual survives almost anything if it has an owner.

risks.risk: The paper says one thing and reality another
risks.sign: Onboarding conditions that were never applied; "configured" limits that don't exist; the showable folder with prop documents
risks.fix: The rule that authorizing with conditions requires applying them the same day, and the audit checking one random condition every month. Paper governance is worse than none: it gives false confidence with a letterhead.

pricing.note: The inventory with the surprises that surface is the deliverable that sells the rest: few leaders see their real picture without shifting in their seat.

pricing.note: Includes the team communication session: a policy explained in person is half the policy. Account migration usually uncovers extra hours: scope it by number of systems.

pricing.note: The price variable is inventory size and the state of the accounts. Ask for the picture before quoting a figure; if there isn't one, sell them the diagnostic first.

pricing.note: Governance decays through abandoning the ritual, not technical failure. This light follow-up is the project's life insurance and an honest recurring income.

defend.question: Isn't this just bureaucracy that'll slow the team down?
defend.answer: The design says the opposite and it's measured: the policy fits on one page, most uses are allowed without asking anything (the matrix says so in ten seconds), and requesting something new costs a two-minute form with an answer in under three days, a deadline audited every month. The kit's litmus test is exactly that: if asking permission cost more than skipping it, governance would have failed and we'd see it in the inventory.

defend.question: What happens to what people were already using on their own?
defend.answer: Amnesty, and it was the first decision: what surfaced into the inventory had no consequences for anyone, because without that promise the inventory would have come out false and we'd be governing a fiction. What surfaced got sorted: the harmless got logged, the improvable got migrated to corporate accounts, and the dangerous triplet (sensitive data on a free tool with a personal account) got attacked in the first week.

defend.question: How do you know spend doesn't get away from you?
defend.answer: Three layers: every paid system has its limit or alert configured at the provider's dashboard (noted where, row by row), actual spend is logged monthly against budget at the audit, and the alerts have been tested with a drill: we lowered an alert on purpose and checked it reached someone who can act. Since it's been in place: [n] billing shocks. The goal is for that number to stay zero.

defend.question: And if there's a data incident tomorrow?
defend.answer: There's a procedure and there's a trail. The procedure: it's reported the same day (the incident log doesn't hunt for culprits and the team knows it from experience), it's evaluated for whether it needs reporting (with this house's sensitive data, the 72-hour window is written down), and whatever the incident teaches gets changed. The trail: the inventory says which system touched what data with what provider and what contract, which is exactly the first thing an investigator asks for. The difference between a bad day and a catastrophe is having that written down beforehand.

defend.question: Who decides what gets approved, an AI?
defend.answer: No: a named person, within a public deadline, and it's logged who and when. The AI prepares the file (checks the request against our policy and proposes a ruling and conditions), which makes deciding cost two minutes instead of an afternoon of digging. But the design is deliberate: a person presses the button, and sensitive-data requests can't even be approved in a hurry.

defend.question: Does this survive when the person running it changes?
defend.answer: It's proven, not promised: the second monthly audit was run by someone else with the operations sheet in front of them, unassisted. The ritual is thirty minutes a month with a checklist and minutes, the keys follow the two-person rule, and the succession risk sits in the risk log itself with leadership as owner. Governance that depends on one person is a hobby; this one is designed to be a house habit.

words: governance
The set of rules, logs and rituals that make sure the house's AI is used with judgment: who, what, with what data, at what cost, and who's accountable.
shadow AI
The use of AI tools without the organization's knowledge. It's not fought by banning it: it's fought by making the official path easier.
amnesty
The promise that reporting what was already being used has no consequences. Without it, the inventory comes out false and governance governs a fiction.
inventory
The list of every AI system and use with its owner, data, account and cost. You can't govern what you can't see.
red list
Your house's specific data that never gets pasted into any AI tool. It's what people remember at the moment of pasting.
permissions matrix
The table crossing roles with data levels that answers "can I use this?" in ten seconds. The policy made checkable.
onboarding circuit
The official path for requesting a new tool or use: a short request, evaluation, and a decision logged within a public deadline.
spending limit
The cap or alert configured at the provider that warns before the shock on the bill. It's set on onboarding day, not the day of the upset.
risk log
The living list of what can go wrong, with impact, probability, mitigation and owner. A risk with no owner is the one that materializes some August.
near-miss
The scare that didn't turn into harm. The cheapest learning material there is: all the lesson, none of the cost.
